why: The migrations are effectively identical, so the decision turns on the system-level judgment, where B reaches further and ranks better: the model swap is correctly put first as the dominant lever, Flex is actually measured on both tiers and deliberately left alone, and B is the only one to reach rework scale with proposals that are specific to llmcord — Router as a first-class provider so /model becomes the catalog, a token budget on the replayed 25-message history (the shipped caps allow ~$3 of input per turn under one spend cap), and replacing the VISION_MODEL_TAGS substring guess with catalog capability flags, a latent bug B found and patched rather than worked around. A is the better migration engineer — it caught that the Dockerfile would ship an image without router_runtime.py (B's image is missing both the runtime and its own router_policy.py) and documented exactly which config.yaml parameters the Responses translation drops — but its improvements all live at the scale of fields on one request, and its two unbuilt items are a declined label split and the same host-unlock B also lists.
A_best: Honesty and operational completeness: the Dockerfile COPY fix (with the correct nuance that compose bind-mounts hid it), and a README that states precisely which per-model parameters survive the Router path, which are dropped silently, which force the request back to OpenAI, and that error shape changes.
B_best: The rework-level diagnosis: VISION_MODEL_TAGS is a substring guess that silently drops image attachments for any new model family (gpt-6-luna today), and the structural fix is the Router catalog's per-model capability flags — paired with the router-as-provider proposal that turns the app's six keys into one and makes the model menu the catalog, with the key-unset 404 loss correctly stated.
A_worst: Its system-level review stops at the single request's fields — no item questions the app's structure (no cap on the replayed history despite naming 25-message replay as the cost driver, no catalog-driven capability handling, no Router-as-provider), and its own text calls the cheap default 'the item I would push hardest' while ranking it fourth; it also leans on a ':vision' model-id suffix to sneak past VISION_MODEL_TAGS instead of fixing the guess.
B_worst: It shipped the same Dockerfile gap A caught — a plain docker build produces an image with neither router_runtime.py nor router_policy.py, so routing silently no-ops — and it documents the migration's parameter-translation losses far less concretely than A; four of its seven improvements are unbuilt, including the two most ambitious.
